description: Wing history states Echo shutdown at 0845 on 16 Mar 1967: all 10 LFs lost strategic alert nearly simultaneously; 'normal controlled shutdown'; faults VRSA ch.9 (G&C No-Go) and ch.12 (Logic Coupler No-Go).
provenance: SRC002 (RR0 transcription of 341 SMW history Apr-Jun 1967, p.33ff)

description: Same wing history: 'external generated signals' judged possible by the investigation team but 'very remote'; only identified mechanism was coupler self-test command + partial reset; further study referred to contractor.

Wing history records power fluctuation at E-1 at 1453 on 16 Mar 1967, commercial power restored 1921; Fergus Electric attributed it to transformer short at Winifred substation. Also a similar Alpha Flight shutdown on 19 Dec 1966 with same capsule crew and weather/power failure.

Wing history says UFO rumors for Echo were 'disproven' and a Mobile Strike Team checking November Flight LFs reported nothing unusual — conflicts with testimony that crews saw UFOs near Echo LFs; interview sourcing of that statement undocumented.
provenance: SRC002 p.37 (citing Engineering Investigation Report p.27)

description: Klotz & Salas (1996) place Salas at November Flight on 16 Mar 1967 (4-5 missiles faulted), whereas the book (2008) places Salas at Oscar Flight on 'probably March 24' with 6-8 missiles — an internal inconsistency in the testimony chronology.

Hastings states the engineering report was 'never made available' and Salas says AF told Boeing/Ogden team head not to write a final report; but the wing history cites an Engineering Investigation Team report dated 23 Mar 1967 (which exists, classified Secret) and says contractor follow-up study was planned.
Kingston George (SI 1993): film debrief and secrecy cautions occurred; film later destroyed; supports existence of a classified filming and of a debrief, differs on interpretation and date (22 Sep).

Launch lists show Atlas D 245D ABRES LORV-3 RV test on 15 Sep 1964 15:27 UTC (08:27 PDT) as a PARTIAL FAILURE (manual cutoff after SECO); book cites 'Atlas D 245H'. A launch malfunction is an untested alternative explanation for a warhead falling short.

Time discrepancy: book (from EA) gives 22 Sep 1964 NTMP KX-19 launch at 13:08 GMT; Wikipedia list gives 15:27 UTC for 22 Sep (identical to 15 Sep) — likely data error; sunrise vs launch-time consistency (George says pre-dawn) not resolved.
Official contemporaneous wording for Loring 27 Oct 1975: 'unidentified helicopter' (TWZ, secondary) / 'A/C' penetration (NMCC teletype quoted by NICAP); Hastings and NICAP treat it as UFO incursion.

FBI 31 Jan 1949 memo exists (3 pp, San Antonio office to Director); describes Top Secret treatment of 'Flying Discs' and Los Alamos concentration; also, per ufopedia, FBI Asst Dir Ladd recommended Bureau decline Army requests because many reports were pranks — context omitted by the book.
Halt memo dating error acknowledged by both book and Wikipedia: first event ~0300 on 26 Dec 1980 (memo says 27 Dec); lighthouse and fireball explanations cited by sceptics.

Chadwell memo quotations appear verbatim in a curated excerpt page; CIA Reading Room text not obtained; a CIA release dated 9 Dec 1952 and Deputies' meeting notes (12 Dec) show DCI Smith was not satisfied with the memo (search summary only).

Quintanilla's 13 Nov 1968 statement is verbatim in the Tulien report; it ALSO states 'The physical violation of the lock of OSCAR 7 does not seem to be related to UFOs'. The book's summary of the Minot case omits the Oscar-7 intrusion.

Base Ops dispatcher entries: 'LATER SIGHTINGS OF BRIGHT LIGHTS AND FLASHING GREEN AND WHITE LIGHTS ACCOMPANIED BY A LOW JET ENGINE SOUND CORRELATES WITH THE B-52 MAKING A VOR PENETRATION, LOW APPROACH AND MISSED APPROACH' (Col. Werlich comment, per Tulien). Supports a conventional-aircraft explanation for part of the ground sightings; book does not mention it.
RAPCON line: 'Somebody is seeing flying saucers again' (Tulien transcript) vs book 'Someone is seeing flying saucers again' — minor quotation variance.
Arithmetic: two miles in one 3-second sweep = 2,400 mph, not 3,900 mph; Tulien states the 3,900 mph figure came from the 14-frame sequence. The book's stated derivation is internally inconsistent.

Florida Today column text (Gross copy) matches the book on Nelson (Site 9, 'guards were scared', could not leave post), Caplan (dimmed lights, OSI interrogation) and Lamb (did not see anything). Column notes three Atlas silos were destroyed by fuel explosions at Walker, a stressful context. Hastings dates the column June 2001; copy index says Oct 2001 — date unresolved.

Atlas deployment facts: Wikipedia lists 579th SMS at Walker AFB (12 Atlas F, 30 Nov 1962-5 Jan 1965) — consistent with book; but states first operational Atlas squadron went on alert at F.E. Warren in Sept 1959 with 6 Atlas D; Warren total 15 (6+9) and Offutt 9 match book; the book's '31 Oct 1959 at Vandenberg' and '6 at Vandenberg' do not match this source.

Condon Report comparison: Wikipedia confirms quoted Low memo text and committee members (incl. Hartmann, Wertheimer, Levine); report 965 pp paperback/1,485 hardcover; also notes consultant Rothberg 'about 100 cases, three or four puzzling' and critics that enigmatic cases were 'buried'. Book's '91 sightings' and 'nearly 30%' not confirmed here.

Frazier: Wikipedia says he worked full-time at Sandia 1983-2006 writing about its research and editing the Sandia Lab News for the last 11 years; consistent with book's 'two decades'; Wikipedia biography itself discloses Sandia, though the SI masthead may not.
Hastings' Ch13 argues the identity/affiliation of skeptics undermines their conclusions (genetic/ad hominem reasoning). It contains no new incident evidence; its value is argumentative.

Werlich's Memo for the Record (24 Oct 1968), quoted by Shough: 'Initially the target traveled approximately 2½ mile in 3 sec or at about 3,000 mi/hr' (arithmetic: 2.5 mi/3 s = 3,000 mph). His 29 Oct telex instead says an echo closed from 3 mi to ~1 mi off the left wing, with no speed. The Blue Book file therefore has TWO different official speed statements; neither is '2 miles in 3 s = 3,900 mph'.
provenance: SRC023 (quoting Blue Book file); verification of original memo pending

description: Origin of '3,900': Shough reconstructs it as the simple average of two rates computed from echo displacements relative to the B-52 between frames 771-772 and 772-773, using antenna paint-time-corrected intervals (3.8 s and 1.3 s): ~1,990 kt and ~5,870 kt, co-altitude upper limits, mean ~3,900 KNOTS (~4,450 statute mph). Hence Clark's number is knots, a mean of very unequal rates, an upper limit, and not '2 miles per sweep'.

Analyst recomputation (this project): from Shough's measured echo positions (771: 138 deg/1.62 NM; 772: 242 deg/1.05 NM; 773: 40 deg/1.05 NM; azimuth from nose, slant range) the displacements are 2.13 and 2.06 NM. With a naive 3.0 s per frame: ~2,560 and ~2,470 kt (~2,950/2,850 mph) relative speed. With Shough's paint-time intervals (3.8, 1.3 s): ~2,020 kt and ~5,710 kt (matches Shough ~1,990/5,870 within ~3%); their simple mean is ~3,865 kt (reproducing '3,900'), but the time-weighted mean over the 5.1 s is only ~2,960 kt (~3,400 mph). Script: database/build/analysis/minot_speed.py.
provenance: Derived from SRC023 numerical values; not independent measurement of the photographs

description: Assumptions behind any speed figure: (i) the three echoes are one target (Shough: cannot be justified from two possibly unrelated echoes; elongated echoes are suggestive but not conclusive); (ii) co-altitude (a depression angle lowers true separation; e.g. at 50 deg the naive horizontal speed would be ~1,650 kt, ~1,900 mph); (iii) range scale inferred (~5 NM display, no indicator on photographs); (iv) only 14 of probably >100 frames survive. The result is an upper-limit estimate, not a measurement of a 3,900 mph object.

[SUPERSEDED by EVD034] Timeline dispute between analysts: Shough concludes frames 771-783 were taken late in the event near the missed approach (so the 'fast' echo transit is not the start); Poher concludes the radarscope clock (0906Z) runs ~9 min ahead of the approach-controller clock so frames coincide with radio loss at ~0858 COM when the B-52 was ~21 nm out (early). The question of when the high-speed transit occurred relative to ground sightings is unresolved in the sources I read.

[PARTLY SUPERSEDED by EVD040] Dispatcher log vs B-52 explanation: entries 0828-0830Z mention jet engines; the B-52 low approach/missed approach was ~0904-0917 COM (Poher). So the Blue Book statement that 'later sightings ... correlate with' the B-52 low approach is plausible for entries after ~0900Z but not demonstrated for the 0800-0858Z entries; and entries 0940-1010Z (after the log says the B-52 landed at 0940Z) describe a stationary object west of N-7 on/near the ground, which the B-52 cannot explain.

Analyst astronomical check (this project; simple GMST/precession, Minot AFB 48.42N 101.36W, 24 Oct 1968): Sirius altitude 11-23 deg, azimuth 132-162 deg (SE to SSE) from 0800Z to 1010Z; Vega 7 deg->-2 deg altitude, azimuth 325-348 deg (NW-NNW), setting ~0940Z. Dispatcher entries 0800Z 'S/E of N-7' fit Sirius direction; entries 0940-1010Z 'west of N-7' do not (~110 deg off); Blue Book cites Vega at azimuth 345 at 0435 local (matches my 342 deg) but the pilot's light was 'west-northwest' (~50 deg away) - requires check of the AF Forms 117. Script: database/build/analysis/minot_sirius.py.
provenance: Computed; positions accurate to ~0.5 deg; atmospheric refraction ignored

description: Blue Book's own text (SRC025) says no data were submitted for the possible 0335 local air visual and 0352 weather-radar paint, and that the pilot's Form 117 puts his sighting at ~0435 local, not 0335: official file acknowledges data gaps in the timeline; Hastings' narrative does not.

Transcript time base: COM clock is Zulu (landing 0940Z matches dispatcher log and pilot's request to 'touch down at 40 past'; CDT = Z-5 with DST still in effect on 24 Oct 1968). All earlier 'local time' mismatches in the file are 1-hr/20-min inconsistencies in individual witness entries, not in the transcript.

Transcript 0852: controller says weather radar also sees the object at the B-52's 1:00, 3 miles; B-52 replies 'We have nothing on our airborne radar and I'm in some pretty thick haze'. Omitted from the book's narrative, which says RAPCON was told weather radar tracked the object 'near Bowbells, ND, 38 nm NW' (Bowbells does not appear in the transcript).

Pilot radio reports (transcript 0902/0904): echo at ~1.25-1.5 mi left of the aircraft from 'about the time we left 200 to about 14 [thousand]' and 'till about 10'; radio trouble began 'exactly' then. Together with the ~10-11.5 k ft altitude derived from the photos, this places frames 771-783 in the latter part of the echo episode (about 0858-0902Z), 3-5 min after first report near FL200.

CORRECTION to EVD027: the Shough/Poher 'early vs late' contrast is narrower than I first reported. Both altitude models put the frames at ~10-11.5 k ft MSL, i.e., late in the echo episode and after the FL200 turn; they differ mainly on clock offset (Shough 7-8 min with caveats; Poher 9 min; my linear-descent estimate 5-6 min). The fast transit in frames 771-773 is therefore not the 'initial' fast approach described by Werlich/McCaslin. See documents/minot_1968_timeline.md.

Partin's Form 117 (30 Oct 1968) describes a stationary 'bright orange ball of light' ~15 mi away at 1 o'clock on/just above the ground, 'miniature sun placed on the ground'; it does not mention an oblong shape, windows, or a tubular section. Those details appear in later interviews quoted by the book (Partin: 'oblong ... windows'; Runyon: barn-sized with a tube, 32 yrs later). The form's sketch shows a small circle with 'a very dim ring of soft white light'.

Partin's reported time (0430-0435 CDT = 0930-0935Z) does not match the transcript (downwind leg 0910Z = 0410 CDT; final 0928Z); the file's annotation 'should be 0335 CDT' (an hour earlier) matches neither. Blue Book used 0435 for its Vega calculation.

Vega test of the Blue Book 'air visual' explanation (analyst calculation): bearing OK — Partin's 1 o'clock from heading 290 magnetic is ~328-332 deg true (declination 8-12 E) vs Vega az 336-337 deg at 0906-0910Z. Brightness FAILS — Vega was only ~1.4 deg->0.4 deg high (airmass 23-33): extinction ~4.6-6.9 mag at 0906Z (k 0.2-0.3), so Vega would appear ~mag 5-7 or fainter, not a 'bright orange ball'/'miniature sun'. Also the light 'remained stationary as we flew toward it' and the aircraft passed ~1 mi south of it, which a star cannot do. A terrestrial light (e.g., ground light, other aircraft) or misjudged range is more consistent than Vega.
provenance: Computed; positions ~0.5 deg; extinction coefficients assumed

description: Ground-observer forms: Smith — reddish burnt orange, twinkling like a star, slight green, on the horizon, ~15 deg elevation, no edges (compass mark appears S-SW; Sirius was SE-SSE: low-res reading, needs checking); O'Connor — white ball -> dim green -> dim amber, facing south, final mark ESE-SE at ~20 deg (matches Sirius direction/elevation) and a Blue Book annotation 'Characteristic colors of Sirius'; Isley — lights 'like head lights or landing lights' on the front and a green flashing light toward the middle or rear, shape/size not determinable, two objects at one time (more aircraft-like); Bond — point of light with fuzzy edges ~10 mi from N-7, two objects, second seen ~3 min, Mohall town lights 4 mi. The observers' descriptions are not uniform: some fit a scintillating Sirius, one suggests an aircraft.

Internal conflict in the file: transcript 0913Z says missile-site personnel 'don't see anything anymore'; dispatcher entries 0940-1010Z say N-7 still sees an object 3 mi west, stationary near the ground. Different sites/time bases are not established.

CORRECTION to EVD028: the transcript shows the B-52 was in the Minot area around 0828-0834Z ('TA calibration check to rw 11', climbing out on heading 290 at 0834), so the 0828-0830Z 'jet engines heard' entries may well be the B-52 — partly supporting the Blue Book aircraft explanation for the earliest entries. The post-0940Z entries (object W of N-7 after the B-52 landed) remain unexplained by it.

Origin of the 3,000 mph figure: FTD Memo for the Record 24 Oct 1968 (doc 5) records Lt Col Werlich's telephone account: 'At about 0300 hours local, a B-52 ... 39 miles northwest of Minot ... sighted an unidentified blip on their radar. Initially the target traveled approximately 2½ mile in 3 sec or at about 3,000 mi/hr.' The memo also says 14 other people in separate locations reported a similar object, and that Werlich did not yet know whether ground observers had looked at stellar bodies. The speed is therefore a verbal, same-day estimate relayed second-hand. Note the stated time (~0300 local) is ~1 h earlier than the transcript's radar/radio events (~0358 local).

Werlich's own assessment (doc 12, phone 31 Oct 1968): 'Most of the original sightings were of the aircraft'; 'Almost 80 per cent were looking at the B-52'; the B-52 radar event and visual 'correlated pretty well'; the one he could not identify is the radar/aircraft event; the air-visual location (TACAN 320 radial, 16 NM) is farm fields with 'nothing there that would produce this type of light'; base lights are visible 50 miles away; the crew could receive but not transmit and used IDENT squawks; 'it couldn't be a malfunction because they transmitted before and afterwards'; scope photos were not taken at first, 'until the pilot said why don't you take some photos. This was towards the end.' The book presents Werlich's data but not his opinion that most ground sightings were the B-52.

Oscar-7 intrusion (doc 12): Werlich says the padlock/combination door had been opened; three similar occurrences in the previous 2-3 years were all traced to Air Police who had been in the service on those areas; '99 chances out of 100' it was someone with a key; a lieutenant found no car/tire/footprint evidence next day; local authorities investigating; Werlich planned to survey with a Geiger counter. The book does not mention the intrusion or the prior look-alike cases.

Pressure to play down: FTD memo 30 Oct 1968 (doc 10) — Col Pullen (HQ SAC) asked Quintanilla for a preliminary report 'so that he could give it to General Stewart to get this thing simmered down' and to 'hit a little heavy on what has happened to other aircraft on occasions like this, this would help play the issue down.' Quintanilla also tells Pullen he suspects an internal radar malfunction or inversion-caused anomalous blip and celestial scintillation, sent nobody (staff of four), and had not yet received times. TWX 1 Nov (doc 25) calls the case 'fairly routine' and 'most probably a plasma of the ball-lightning class' before raw data arrived; SAC TWX 7 Nov (doc 26) says the SAC commander and staff were 'extremely interested.' Supports the book's theme that the Air Force evaluation was hasty and shaped by command interest, though the Blue Book memos also show attempts to get data (doc 11).

Doc 15 (Werlich's list of ground observers; 0308-0325 local) repeats that SSgt Smith at Oscar-1 'saw the object separate in two parts and go in opposite directions and return and pass under each other,' with a handwritten Blue Book comment: 'Smith does not say this on 117.' My reading of Smith's AF 117 agrees (reddish burnt orange light 'as a star might twinkle,' no separation). The book (12835-12840) relays the separation detail from the Wing Security Controller's summary via Tulien without this caveat. Isley, Adams and Jablonski forms do mention two objects approaching and one disappearing.

Weather-radar evidence: the transcript (0852) says the weather radar also saw the object, but Blue Book staff phoned Minot on 8 and 13 Nov 1968 specifically to ask about the weather radar and could not reach Werlich (docs 27, 29). No weather-radar record or description appears in the case-file documents I read; the book's 'Bowbells, 38 nm NW' detail is not in them.

Project 10073 record (doc 3): observation 24/0030-0530Z (4 h 48 min); photos: No; conclusions — ground visual 'Probable (AIRCRAFT) (B-52)' and 'Probable Astro (SIRIUS)'; radar 'Possible (PLASMA)'; air-visual 'Possible (PLASMA)'. The official record is therefore a mixed aircraft/star/plasma attribution, not a single cause.

Independent measurement (analyst, scans at 300 ppi): ring peaks in frame 771 at 60/134/208 px (74 px = 0.5 NM, i.e. 148 px/NM) and hole edge 266 px = 2.14 NM with Shough's offset — matching Shough's 2.1 NM. Strongest local blobs: frame 772 at 1.09 NM (Shough 1.05), screen angle 124 deg; frame 773 at 1.08 NM (Shough 1.05), 282 deg. Angular separation 158 deg equals Shough's. Displacement 2.14 NM (Shough 2.06, +4%).

Sensitivity to range-scale calibration: with Shough's offset (rings at 0.75/1.25/1.75 NM) the 772->773 displacement is 2.14 NM = ~2,565 kt at 3.0 s or ~5,920 kt at 1.3 s; if instead range is linear from the centre (rings at 0.5/1.0/1.5 NM) the displacement is 1.46 NM = ~1,750 kt at 3.0 s or ~4,040 kt at 1.3 s. The unexplained calibration (no scale indicator on the photos) therefore shifts speeds by ~30%.

Frame 771 (half-swept): the reported echo at 1.62 NM lies on/inside the third range ring; azimuthal ring-brightness profile shows only small variations (peak 135-140 vs ring ~80-95 at 4-20 deg screen angle) that I cannot separate from ring noise. I could NOT independently confirm that echo. The 771->772 displacement (and the '1,990 kt' rate) therefore rests on Shough's identification.

AF Forms 117 of Adams and Jablonski (viewed at low resolution): Adams — head lights/lights at an air facility; lights reddish orange changing to white and green, self-luminous, very bright, size/shape hard to distinguish; annotation 'see characteristic colors of Sirius'; en route to N-7 another object appeared; they came close then one disappeared; compass A at ~SE. Jablonski — two objects dispatched to N-7; one at the same speed moving toward the other, one vanished; glowing orange-red, white, greenish; 'rather solid', 'very wide and slender', edges fuzzy, 'much brighter than a star'; annotation 'Sirius has m of -1.6'. Combined with Isley and Bond: the maintenance/security observers describe two lights converging with one disappearing — compatible with Sirius plus the B-52, or a pair of aircraft, but not established.

The 90th SMW's own report to FTD (SRC032) counts 148 objects reported by 143 personnel over three nights (31 Jul 75/70; 1 Aug 29/27; 2 Aug 44/46) — about one 'object' per observer — and describes them as mostly round, pinhead-to-nickel sized with colored lights flashing every 1-2 seconds, in V/echelon/cross/box formations, silent. The book, which relies on the Anspaugh log, does not mention this report, its counts, or these descriptors (checked by text search). Analyst note: scintillation-like flashing, star-like angular sizes and the mass-reporting pattern are what one expects from stars/planets under an inversion; they do not rule out something else.

Blue Book addendum of 20 Sep 1965 (SRC033): contemporaneous binocular and 40x-theodolite observations (Sioux Army Depot guard; nine military observers; Geodetic Survey Team) describe star-sized or pinhead-sized objects, some moving, and on four occasions 'a roaring jet-like noise at some distance behind' — contradicting the 6 Aug report's 'no sound' and suggesting aircraft in at least some cases. The theodolite observation (object in the Big Dipper resolving to three white objects) is an instrumented one rarely seen in such cases. Book does not mention these.

A skeptical reviewer's reading of the Blue Book file (SRC034): reports were short, lacked positional data, clustered ~0500Z (2300 MDT), and plausibly involve Jupiter, Capella, Saturn, Vega, Altair, Betelgeuse, Echo 2 and aircraft under an inversion; Blue Book never assigned specific explanations to individual Warren reports; a Blue Book sergeant (Moody) asked for positional data and was ignored. This supports BOTH sides in part: the 'stars' label was weakly supported (Blue Book gave no case-by-case identification) yet the file also lacks any positional data to prove anything else.

[PARTLY CORRECTED by EVD061 — Eastern-time conclusion was wrong: Pleiades/Aldebaran omitted] Analyst sky test (PyEphem 4.2.1; Cheyenne 41.15N 104.82W; script warren_sky_1965.py), 1 Aug 1965. If the Anspaugh log times are Mountain (Warren local): Jupiter (mag -1.9) rose ~0300 and stood at alt 9-13 deg, az 68-71 deg at 0317-0340; Aldebaran alt 15-19 deg az 81-85; Capella alt 26-29 az 50-53; Saturn alt ~41 az 175-182; Vega alt 37-41 az 290-292; Deneb alt 61-65. The 0340 entry 'one UFO at 70 deg azimuth' matches Jupiter's azimuth (71 deg); 'seven/six UFOs east' (0320-0325) and 'five going east' (Sioux Depot 0335) lie in the direction of Jupiter/Aldebaran/Capella; at 0400 'four NW, three NE' fits Vega/Deneb (WNW) and Capella/Jupiter (NE). But entries at 0130-0250 MDT have only Saturn, Capella (low NE), Vega, Altair, Deneb, Fomalhaut — no Jupiter. If the log times are Eastern (WPAFB; 2 h earlier locally) every entry falls before Jupiter rose and the match fails (Jupiter and Aldebaran not yet above the horizon). The time zone of the log is not stated in the book; Printy's '~0500Z' cluster (2300 MDT = 0100 EDT) fits the Eastern reading for the first entries. The test is therefore suggestive for some entries under one assumption, inconclusive overall.

[Time zone resolved in part by EVD059: most probably Eastern] Log internal timing: the Anspaugh entries mix call times and event times (e.g., 4:05 call about a 4:00 report; 4:40 call about 3:00 and 3:17 reports; later entries 3:20-3:40 follow the 4:40 call). Entries are not in chronological order and carry no time zone, so whether they are Eastern (Blue Book) or Mountain (Warren) cannot be determined from the text I have. The original memorandum and Hynek's printing (UFO Experience, 1972) were not examined.

Bolender document: the key sentence is verbatim in NICAP's transcription ('reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system (Atch 10)'). Differences from the book: NICAP calls it a draft, not a memorandum; whether it was signed or sent to all commands is not shown; the 16 attachments are missing; the same document says there is no evidence Blue Book reports served any intelligence function. The sentence supports 'national-security reports are outside Blue Book' but does not show that nuclear-site UFO reports existed in those channels.

Ch.16 states Blue Book 'blithely dismissed the sighting reports at each base as having no merit.' For Minot the file shows otherwise: Blue Book assigned aircraft/Sirius/plasma attributions, labelled the radar and air-visual 'possible plasma', and the file records SAC pressure to play the issue down (EVD044) — so the process was influenced, but the stated conclusions were specific explanations, not blanket dismissal. For Warren, Blue Book's disposition was 'insufficient data'/stars/'inversion effect' with no case-by-case identification (EVD054).

Hynek (1972, p.233) prints the log as calls 'received at the Blue Book offices by Lieutenant Anspaugh' (Dayton, Ohio), and the book's version matches it. The call times are therefore the Blue Book (Eastern) clock. The batch of events passed on in the 4:40 call (H-2 3:00; B-4 3:17; 3:20-3:40) all precede that call, which is only consistent if they are on the same clock: if they were Warren local (MDT, 1-2 h behind Eastern) they would postdate the 4:40 call. Inference: the whole log is most probably Eastern (EDT or EST) — it is not Mountain time. This resolves the time-zone question except for EST vs EDT.

Hynek's commentary: Blue Book dismissed the Midwest flap as 'stars seen through inversion layers'; Quintanilla said the Warren sightings were 'nothing but stars!' (CLM100 now matched to Hynek's text); Hynek argues inversions cannot make stars move through a considerable arc. But he then sets out two competing hypotheses — a cover-up, and a 'foul-up' based on the premise that the reports could not have a basis in fact — and adds that Blue Book's 'lack of interest belies any charge of cover-up; they just didn't care.' The book (Ch.10, Ch.16) uses the 'stars' quote and calls the Warren handling 'patently absurd,' but not Hynek's lack-of-interest reading.

CORRECTION to EVD055 and updated sky test (analysis/warren_sky_by_entry.py; stars/planets incl. the Pleiades; times shifted by hypothesis H0 Mountain, H1 EST, H2 EDT). Eastern readings (H1/H2, the likely ones per EVD059): '3:00 white oval directly overhead' -> Deneb at 78-86 deg altitude (H0: no bright object >70 deg); '3:20 seven UFOs east' and '3:25 six stacked vertically' -> the Pleiades (six-seven naked-eye stars) low in the ENE at 8-19 deg (and Aldebaran 4-5 deg under H1); '3:40 one at 70 deg azimuth' -> Pleiades/Aldebaran at az 68-77 deg; '4:00 four NW, three NE' -> Vega/Deneb (WNW) and Capella plus the Pleiades (NE). Jupiter only matters under Mountain time (H0), which EVD059 makes unlikely. My earlier statement that the match 'fails' under Eastern time was wrong because I omitted the Pleiades and Aldebaran.

[(b) CORRECTED by EVD069: fainter stars exist near az 120] Log entries NOT explained by stars/planets in my test: (a) 3:17 'oval and white with white lines on its sides and a flashing red light in its center moving east ... descending ... landed 10 miles east' — describes an aircraft with anti-collision beacon and wing lights more than a star; (b) 3:40 'one at 120 deg' — no bright star/planet near azimuth 120 deg at 1:40-3:40 MDT under any hypothesis (Saturn is at ~140 deg); (c) '4:00 four NW' — only Vega and Deneb are bright NW; (d) 'three came from the east, stacked vertically, passed through the other two, all five heading west' — an apparent-motion description that would require illusory motion (autokinesis/scintillation) or aircraft; (e) 1:30 'large circular object emitting several colors ... moved rapidly to the northeast' (Cheyenne civilians, 2330-0130 MDT) — Capella low in the NE is the only bright star there; aircraft/meteors/satellites more likely.

[SUPERSEDED by EVD064-EVD066: Echo 2 test done using SAO 1965 mean elements; Echo 1 also checked] Satellite (Echo 2) test NOT done: no 1965 orbital elements were available to me. Feasibility note: Echo 2 (~1,000-1,300 km altitude) can be sunlit overhead only while the sun is < ~33 deg below the horizon; at Cheyenne on 1 Aug the sun reaches ~-31 deg at ~0100 MDT, so passes between ~2300 and ~0200 MDT would be marginal and after ~0200 MDT well lit. Whether any pass coincided with a log entry requires historical TLEs (Space-Track login).

Echo 2 on the night of the log (analysis/warren_echo2_passes.py, from SAO mean elements; the two element sets agree to ~10 s): three visible passes over Cheyenne on 1 Aug 1965 UTC — P1 0502-0508Z (peak 10 deg, E->NE), P2 0650-0659Z (peak 66 deg, az 118->97->14: rising ESE, peaking in the east, ending N), P3 0839-0848Z (peak 25 deg, W->NNW). In printed-clock terms: H0 Mountain 2302/0050/0239 MDT; H1 EST 0002/0150/0339; H2 EDT 0102/0250/0439. Echo 1 has no visible pass in the window (its only geometric pass, ~0321-0335Z, precedes it).

Coincidence with log entries (analysis/warren_echo2_coincidence.py): with +-3 min slack, H0 matches 1 entry (2:50), H1 matches 3 (1:48, 1:49, 3:40), H2 matches 3 (2:50, 3:00, 4:40 [a call time]). A random shift of the clock gives a mean of 1.9 of 18 entries inside pass windows (P(>=3) ~ 0.26), so the Echo 2 matches are NOT significant. Qualitatively: under H1 the 1:48-1:49 'same formation at G and E flights' coincides with P2's rise in the ESE and 3:40 sits in P3 but P3 runs W->N, not 'heading west'; under H2 '2:50 nine more UFOs' and '3:00 white oval directly overhead' coincide with P2 (peak 66 deg, east), which is a better fit to 'overhead' than Deneb only if the observer judged 66 deg as overhead.

Echo 2 cannot explain the log's multi-object or crossing-motion entries: it is a single object crossing the sky in ~5-9 visible minutes at ~0.1-0.3 deg/s, silent, steady, brightness ~ +1 to +2.5. It is a candidate for isolated 'moving light' entries only. Printy's review lists Echo 1/2 and other satellites as generators of reports across the whole Aug 1965 flap; that is plausible but, for Warren, unproven.

The book's moon detail therefore contradicts the astronomical record for the stated date; either the date or the lunar description (as relayed from the anonymous report) is wrong. Version matrix of Salas's public accounts (via SRC001, SRC042, SRC043, book): (1) Aug 1996 emails to Fowler: already decided it was 'November' after the wing history; commander not yet named. (2) Nov 1996 Klotz/Salas article: Echo Flight, 16 Mar 1967, 4-5 missiles, flight designation uncertain. (3) 1 Oct 1996 Meiwald letter: 'Our home site was Oscar'; guards saw the 'UFO', radio lost, two upset men; no injury recalled; no missile failures described in the quoted text. (4) 1997 MUFON: November Flight; Meiwald recalled about 5 of 10 shut down. (5) Dec 2000: Meiwald 'maybe seven or eight'. (6) Faded Giant 2005 / book 2008: Oscar Flight, 'probably March 24', 6-8 missiles; Echo a separate event ~8 days earlier. (7) 2010 affidavit: Oscar, 'on or about 24 March', all or nearly all ten. Flight: Echo -> November -> Oscar; count: 4-5 -> 5 -> 7-8 -> 6-8 -> 10; date: 16 Mar -> ~24 Mar. Per Carlson, Salas asserted November until 1999-2000.

Settlement of the November-vs-Oscar question: it is not documentary. Only one flight, Oscar, comes from the other crew member (Meiwald, 1996 letter, as quoted by Carlson), and he later said he remembers little (per Carlson); Salas moved from Echo to November to Oscar as new information arrived. The only contemporaneous record located (SRC002) documents one shutdown, at Echo, 16 Mar 1967, 0845, and says UFO rumors were disproven. Best statement: the Oscar attribution rests on Meiwald's 1996 recollection and Salas's later adoption of it; no log or roster has been seen. Echo/Oscar conflation remains open (EXP039).

Wikipedia's 'Malmstrom' page states Sheaffer's reading: UFO at Oscar probably Mars with no missiles off; Echo an electronic glitch with no UFO. I did not verify Mars position for any date; the mechanism rests on my reading of a secondary quote, not a calculation.

Mars check at Malmstrom AFB (47.5N 111.2W, MST=UTC-7; analysis/salas_mars_1967.py, PyEphem). Mars was mag -0.7 to -0.8 on 16 Mar 1967 and about -1.0 to -1.1 on 24-25 Mar, i.e. brighter than every star except Sirius, a steady reddish point. Rise ~2115-2145 MST in the ESE, highest (alt ~31-33 deg) ~0230-0300 in the south, set ~0730-0800 in the WSW. At the Echo shutdown time (0845 MST, 16 Mar) Mars was below the horizon and the Sun was up, so Mars cannot be involved in the Echo event. For a night-time Oscar event ~24 Mar, Mars was available from ~2130 to ~0730, but a near-full Moon (95-100%) was also up for most of the night, which neither Salas nor the book mentions. Mars is a point source with no motion relative to the stars; Salas/book describe a ~30-40 ft red oval at the front gate, guards reporting maneuvering lights, and one injured guard. Mars therefore plausibly explains a red light seen low in the sky early in the evening but cannot by itself explain the 'hovering outside the gate' or 'maneuvering' descriptions; the time of the Oscar sighting is not given in the sources I have seen, so the test is inconclusive. This supersedes the untested EVD079.

Meiwald's own words (SRC045). 1996 call with Salas (Salas leads: 'some of our missiles started shutting down. Is that right?'): Meiwald 'Uh huh ... Right. We had security alarms and, uh ... problems at a couple of the, uh, sites.' He recalls two guards who went to an LF, lost radio contact on return, were 'scared to death', relieved of duty; 'they had seen these, some crazy things.' 1 Oct 1996 letter (excerpt): 'Our home site was Oscar'; topside security reported the mobile team saw a 'UFO' near an LF just east of Highway 19 (Grass Range to the Missouri); radio contact lost; 'Two very upset young men'; no personnel injury recalled; the crew 'formed ... Sept 66 in N [status]'. 2011 call with Hastings: recalls being woken, 'unusual indications on the consol', a security violation, team reporting 'unusual activity'; does NOT remember Salas telling him of a bright object at the gate; 'I'm saying I don't remember'; 'We had an incident in October [sic] Flight' (sic by Hastings); recalls missile count as six to eight per Hastings (not in transcript excerpt). So: Meiwald independently affirms Oscar and a team's UFO report at an outlying LF, assents (to a leading question) to missiles shutting down, and does not corroborate the gate object, the injured guard, or the number ten. The Salas gate-object and the Meiwald LF-object are separate reports (Salas, 9 May 2011 email: the second came to Meiwald from the FSC). No date, time, or bearing appears. This partly corrects EVD077/EVD078: Meiwald's letter excerpt alone (as quoted by Carlson) omitted missiles, but the 1996 call shows assent.

Evaluation of Carlson's claim (SRC042) that nowhere does Meiwald link the event he describes with missile failures and that transcripts show nothing of the kind: partly wrong. In the 1996 call Meiwald says 'Uh huh' and 'Right' to the missile-shutdown sequence, though he supplies no detail and the question was leading. Carlson's other points stand: no UFO at the gate, no injury, no date, a minor security alert is a possible reading, the 'N' in Meiwald's letter is crew status and not necessarily a flight (Hastings brackets it as 'November Flight'; the origin of Salas's 'November' is not established from this).

Figel's statements about Echo, per Hastings summaries of three taped calls (SRC046): (a) a guard already at the silo reported 'a large, round object ... directly over the site', 'seconds after' the missile failed; Figel 'was thinking he was yanking my chain', but the guard 'seemed to be serious'; (b) Figel sent two Security Alert Teams, who (2010) reported seeing the hovering UFO although he had not told them what to look for (in 1996, to Salas, both teams reported it; in the 2008 call he once said the first report came from a team, which Hastings calls a misspeak); (c) all ten missiles dropped over 'three or four minutes', not 'within seconds' as Salas wrote; (d) he saw a Channel 9 No-Go in the capsule while a technician (Barlow) says no VRSA code showed at the silos, which Figel concedes may be possible; (e) he kept no personal log, only the official deputy log; (f) 'Thank you very much, don't talk about it, and go home. I didn't sign anything'; (g) he does not believe an Oscar event happened, ascribing Salas's story to 'faulty memory' not malice. Mutual disagreement exists over what Figel said about Carlson: James Carlson says Figel thought the guard was joking; Hastings's excerpt shows Figel believed the guard serious but did not take him seriously. Source quality: Hastings's text only.

Three-way comparison of Echo accounts. Book Ch.5-6 (via Don Crawford, who relieved the crew and was told by Figel, secondhand): maintenance teams at two LFs reported maneuvering lights before dawn, confirmed by a mobile SAT; at ~0830 missiles dropped 'within seconds'; two SATs then went to each LF, found the objects gone, but personnel there reported them hovering near the silos. Figel's taped version (SRC046): a single on-site guard's call after the first missile failed; two SATs later reported seeing the object; no pre-dawn calls appear in Hastings's summaries (and he admits mixing Salas's Oscar 'lights at a distance' call into questions about Echo); failure took 3-4 minutes. Wing history (SRC002): all Echo sites lost alert ~0845 'nearly simultaneously', with 'rumors of UFOs ... disproven' by a Mobile Strike Team that checked November Flight LFs. Differences: timing of reports (pre-dawn vs after failure), source of first report (maintenance at two LFs vs one guard), duration, object location (near silos vs directly over). No contemporaneous log of any UFO report has been seen.

Re-read of the 341st SMW history Echo section (SRC002, rr0 transcription, pp.33-38) for electrical/timing detail. (1) 0845 loss of alert, all ten LFs, VRSA ch.9 and 12 No-Go; no other flight affected. (2) Crew (questioned 16 Mar by DCMET, OOAMA and Boeing) estimated the interval between loss of alert and fault indication at 10-40 seconds and the start of the event no more than 2-3 minutes before the 0845 log time; Figel's 2010 '3-4 minutes' for all ten to drop is longer than the crew's same-day estimate. (3) The deputy was turned away from the console briefing the commander who had just been awakened when the faults appeared; the commander saw them first. This is the same scene Salas and Hastings narrate for Oscar. (4) No electrical equipment in use; E-8 was on diesel (ch.26) and its generator ran intermittently; E-2 door-actuator motor failed. (5) Power events at E-1: transformer short south of Winifred substation at ~1450, fluctuations at 1453 and 1510-1600, commercial power back 1921 - all hours AFTER the 0845 shutdown, so they do not by themselves explain it. (6) Investigation: G&C channel 50 dumps from E-7/E-8 showed shutdown by external influence on G&C, not a G&C No-Go; the Logic Coupler could generate ch.9+12 but only if all ten were affected within seconds or partially reset the same way ('very remote'); weather, EWO, radar (801st RS), PAS and Boeing modification teams (at B-1, K-1, O-1 after the event) ruled out; power switching test of 28 Mar not the cause; 'LCC power fault transmitted on the hardened cable' judged the only power fault capable; no logical cause found. Similar Alpha Flight event 19 Dec 1966 with the same capsule crew. (7) 'Rumors of UFOs ... disproven' rests on a Mobile Strike Team that checked all NOVEMBER Flight LFs that morning; the text does not say Echo LFs were checked or that Echo guards were interviewed. The history itself shows that UFO rumors existed in the wing by mid-1967 (Gamble per the book). The Boeing 'noise injected into the logic coupler' result cited by Klotz in the book is not in this excerpt. The excerpt gives neither confirmation nor refutation of any UFO report from Echo; it does show the cause of the shutdown was officially undetermined.

Correction of an earlier record: EXP035 (Delta-3 Mills explanation) had cited the Echo wing history as showing power fluctuations 'coincident with No-Go'; the history places them ~6 hours after the shutdown (EVD085). EXP035 text corrected at source; the Delta-3 power-loss explanation now rests only on the generic winter-weather argument plus Mills's own report that all power (commercial, diesel, battery) was lost.

Re-reading SRC001 (Klotz/Salas, 27 Nov 1996, NICAP mirror) against the wing history (SRC002): the 1996 article places Salas as DMCCC in NOVEMBER Flight on the morning of 16 March 1967, with a SECOND, separate shutdown of 'four or five' missiles at November 'at or about the same time' as Echo's ten, and describes UFOs seen at the November LCC and one N LF as well as at Echo LFs. SRC002 says 'No other Wing I configuration lost strategic alert at that time' (0845) and that the only mobile team named checked November's LFs and saw nothing. So the 1996 two-flight same-morning version is contradicted by the one contemporaneous record, and the Oscar relocation (2005 on) is partly the repair of that contradiction. The 1996 article also says early-morning reports came from more than one patrol and maintenance crew (Echo) and the missiles shut down 'over the next half-minute' (matching the crew's 10-40 s estimate, not Figel's 2010 3-4 minutes).

Boeing/Klotz reproduction claim: the 1996 article says the effects were reproduced only by directly introducing a 10-volt pulse onto a data line and that this could be done from outside the shielded system only by an electromagnetic pulse of unknown origin; Sparks (NICAP) says Boeing issued the SECRET engineering report. The wing-history excerpt calls an externally generated signal 'very remote' and says no cause was found; it does not mention a 10 V pulse. Neither the full Engineering Investigation Team report (23 Mar 1967) nor Kaminski's 1 Feb 1997 letter to Klotz has been seen by me; I found a blog repost claiming AARO attributed the event to a 'cascading transformer failure' during an 'electrical storm' - unverified and in conflict with the wing history, which ruled out weather and put the transformer short at ~1450. Wikipedia's mention of a 2025 Pentagon EMP report also remains unsupported.

AARO's explanation for Echo, as far as I can establish: only second-hand. Per an advocate email (SRC048), ex-AARO deputy director Phillips said in interviews that a 'cascading transformer failure' triggered by an 'electrical storm' caused the shutdown, while a 6 Jun 2025 WSJ story citing AARO officials reportedly said an unannounced EMP test did; neither is in a primary AARO document that I could open (the Volume I historical report PDF could not be downloaded: 403/empty responses from aaro.mil, media.defense.gov and fas.org). Comparison with the wing history (SRC002): a 7.2 kV transformer did short near Winifred at ~1450 on 16 March, 6 hours after the 0845 shutdown, and the history ruled out weather and power switching as the cause, so a 'transformer cascade' explanation does not fit the timing or the record as transcribed; the same history says no cause was found. Hastings's email says later wing histories (mid-1967 and about a year later) record power tests as 'essentially negative' and speculate an EMP cause; I did not see those histories. An EMP-test explanation is therefore unsupported by any document I have, and the AARO transformer explanation conflicts with the one I have. AARO's actual wording is unknown to me.

AARO Volume I (SRC049), the primary AARO text, says nothing on the cause of the Echo or Oscar shutdowns and does not mention transformers, electrical storms or an EMP test. Its nuclear passage: five former USAF members who served near ICBM silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth, Vandenberg and Minot (1966-77) claim sightings and/or UAP disruption (launch control facilities offline or total power failure); AARO 'investigated and reached conclusions on the majority of the claims'; unresolved allegations deferred to Volume II; only one nuclear-related item is addressed in the findings (the alleged 1964 reentry-vehicle film, not recovered, matched in time/place to an ABM test). It also reports no UAP-specific NDAs found in the records AARO reviewed (apart from standard Title 18 language) - which bears on, but does not refute, the claim that Salas, Meiwald and others signed OSI NDAs (those may be ordinary debrief statements and AARO's search covers only what it found). So the 'transformer cascade' and 'EMP test' statements (EVD089) were made in interviews/press, not in Volume I; Volume II was due later and I could not confirm it exists or what it says. Footnote 98 cites 'AARO case files' (non-public).

(a) Byelokoroviche 4 Oct 1982 (UTC+3): at 1800 MSK Sun alt +5; Venus mag -3.8 alt 5 W-SW (sets ~1900); Jupiter -1.6 alt 13 SW; Saturn alt 10 SW; Mars +0.9 alt 14 S-SW; Moon (97%, waning) rises ENE ~1930-2000 and is up all evening. (b) Kapustin Yar 28-29 Jul 1989 22:12-01:30 (UTC+4): Moon (16-17%) below horizon until ~0100; Venus and Mars set by ~2200-2400; Saturn S alt 18 to 9; Jupiter rises ~0030 NE. No bright astronomical object accounts for a 2-hour low hovering object in the first half of the window. (c) Manzano 8 Aug 1980 2350 MDT: Moon 3% below horizon; Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn all below the horizon: no astronomical explanation. (d) Katta-Kurgan Oct 1984 2345 (UTC+5): date unknown; all bright planets below horizon; the Moon is up on ~3-16 Oct, down 17-31 Oct; no resolution possible; a fireball/reentry is a candidate for a slowly descending hissing object but is not tested.

INF Treaty Memorandum of Understanding (1 Nov 1987 data; fas.org text, SRC050): 'Belokorovichi' (51 10 N 028 03 E) appears as an SS-20 missile operating base with 9 launchers (and a missile storage area), i.e. an intermediate-range base, not an ICBM base as the book says; and Kattakurgan (39 38 N 065 58 E) is listed as an SS-12 operating base with 9 missiles and 5 launchers, matching the book's figures. Kapustin Yar is listed as a test range. These are Nov 1987 figures; presence of SS-20s at Belokorovichi in Oct 1982 is plausible but not shown by this source. Popular accounts of an 'ICBM' launch sequence 'aimed at New York' are not supported by the base type.

The book's description of the R-14: Wikipedia states the R-14 (SS-5 Skean) was withdrawn completely from Soviet service in 1984 (retired in the late 1970s except some soft sites, replaced by the RSD-10 from 1978-83), so 12 R-14s 'operational' at Kapustin Yar in 1989 is wrong; for the Cuban crisis, only 24 R-14 warheads arrived and no missiles or launchers were shipped (the missiles deployed in Cuba were R-12 / SS-4). 'RT-14' is not the designation. Kapustin Yar later hosted other missiles (INF MOU).

Chapter 22-23 evidence structure: DeSisto (INC069) reports no UFOs and Hastings's UFO inference is explicit speculation; Kirtland (INC070) rests on a real AFOSI form but from a quotation; Soviet cases (INC071-INC073) are secondhand through TV and Berliner's summaries of KGB files; I could not locate the ABC Prime Time Live transcript or the KGB files, and search results for the 1982 event mostly concern popular recirculations with conflicting place names (Usovo vs Byelokoroviche).

LOOK 1 July 1952 (SRC052) vs the book's CLM098: the article is by J. Robert Moskin, not Ruppelt; the 63 sightings are Ruppelt's 'most detailed and most mystifying' unidentified cases in general (from pilots, ship observers, a colonel, scientists, weather observers and intelligence officers), not '63 cases of UFOs over nuclear installations.' The article says that when the 63 were mapped, 'a number of concentrations duplicated exactly the area of atomic energy installations', and that intelligence found no pattern/correlation otherwise and no evidence the saucers were spying on atomic plants. So the book's (Aldrich's) wording overstates the 63 as a nuclear-site file; the true statement is that clusters coincided with AEC areas and that the 63 file is not in declassified Blue Book files (the second part I did not test).

USAFE TT #1524 (SRC053) vs CLM099: Aldrich's description of the cable (4 Nov 1948, USAFE A-2 to Air Force DI, copies to CIA and AMC, Swedish lake object) is confirmed in outline by his own article, which I read; the Wikipedia-style 'existence of TS UFO documents at Wright Field' inference is his, and he himself says the Estimate of the Situation is separately unconfirmed. The cable's own content was mostly Neubiberg and Swedish-opinion items; the Swedish lake object is tied by Aldrich to a likely Soviet-origin missile sighting by Gen. Jung (24 Aug 1948), a context the book omits. The original telecon was not seen by me; a War.gov copy (2026 release) was blocked. The book's quoted Saturday Evening Post/Shallet restriction (Secret only, not TS) is from Aldrich's footnote and is not tested.
